Milk pasteurization has been around since the 1800s. Thanks for this go to Louis Pasteur, who demonstrated in the 1860s that abnormal fermentation of wine and beer could be prevented by heating the beverages, and to Frans von Soxhlet, a German agricultural chemist, who in 1886, was the first person to suggest that milk sold to the public be pasteurized. 

The benefits of heating or boiling milk have been recognized since the early 1800s and has been used to reduce milk-borne illness and mortality in infants since the late 1800s. Raw milk can carry dangerous germs, such as brucella, campylobacter, cryptosporidium, E. coli, listeria, and salmonella. Foodborne illnesses such as typhoid, scarlet fever and tuberculosis were virtually eliminated with the commercial implementation of pasteurization.

Here's the exercise prescription I give every patient: minimum of 250 minutes a week. That's about 35 minutes a day. Here's how it breaks down and why.

~150 min/week of moderate cardio. This is the threshold where the data consistently shows lower cardiovascular disease risk (Piercy 2018; Bull/WHO 2020). It's not a magic cliff. Benefit starts below it, but it's the target worth aiming for.

~100 min/week of resistance training. Strength work is what packs the punch for lowering all-cause mortality and blood pressure. Mortality benefit shows up around 60 min/week (Shailendra 2022); I prescribe a bit more to also cover strength, function, and BP.

And if you're a woman, lift. Women tend to get equal or greater longevity benefit at the same, or even lower activity dose than men (Ji 2024, JACC; He 2025, NHANES), and resistance training is linked to lower hypertension risk specifically in women (Park & Park 2024).

So when a patient tells me they've got ~35 minutes a day, I tell them to split it: ~20 minutes of cardio, ~15 minutes of strength. That's the whole prescription. Most of the benefit comes from simply going from doing nothing to doing something.

Educational content, not individual medical advice. Talk to your clinician before starting a new program.

This rapid drop in visual input signals safety to your brain, quickly shifting you into parasympathetic rest-and-digest mode, lowering cortisol, and allowing melatonin production to begin earlier in the evening. 
 
To deepen the sensory reset, add a few drops of calming lavender, pine, ylang ylang or eucalyptus essential oil or a handful of fresh eucalyptus or lavender leaves right under the shower stream—the warm water releases their therapeutic compounds, creating an aromatherapy steam that further calms the nervous system while supporting respiratory and skin health. How I try to avoid food poisoning when I travel ✈️

A few simple habits can lower your risk:

• Wash your hands before you eat. It sounds simple, but germs from stool can easily spread to your hands from bathroom surfaces, door handles, phones, and other frequently touched objects.

• Choose foods that are freshly cooked and served hot. This is especially important in airports, food courts, and buffets.

• Avoid foods that have been sitting out at room temperature, especially meat, seafood, dairy products, rice, and sauces.

One thing many people don’t know is that bismuth subsalicylate has been shown in studies to reduce the risk of travelers’ diarrhea and is included as an option in travel medicine guidelines for some travelers.

However, bismuth is not appropriate for everyone. It can interact with certain medications, including blood thinners, aspirin, and other medications, and may not be safe for people with certain medical conditions. Be sure to discuss it with your healthcare professional before taking it.

Even if you do everything right, food poisoning and travelers’ diarrhea can still happen. But practicing good hand hygiene, choosing freshly cooked foods, and following food safety recommendations can significantly lower your risk while traveling.

This is not medical advice. This post is a review of gastroenterology and travel medicine guidelines for educational purposes only. Always discuss medications with your own healthcare professional before taking them.

Mix them into Greek yogurt, Skyr, kefir, cottage cheese, smoothies, overnight oats, applesauce, oatmeal, pancake batter, muffin batter, banana bread, protein balls, homemade energy bites, soups, sauces, or even stir them into peanut butter or almond butter.

It’s one of the simplest ways to increase your daily fiber intake while supporting gut health, digestive health, bowel regularity, fullness, satiety, and your gut microbiome.

2. Traditional durum wheat semolina pasta. Most dried Italian pasta is made from 100% durum wheat semolina, and it still contains gluten. What makes it different is its dense protein-starch structure, especially when cooked al dente, which slows digestion and helps keep you fuller longer. Some researchers think this may also mean less carbohydrate reaches the colon quickly, which could reduce fermentation and bloating in some people, although that hasn’t been definitively proven. The good news is that brands made with 100% durum semolina are widely available in U.S. grocery stores.

3. Smaller portions. Traditional pasta servings are often much smaller than what many restaurants serve elsewhere.

4. Slower, more intentional eating. Meals are meant to be enjoyed, giving your body more time to recognize fullness before you overeat.

5. More walking and less driving. On vacation you’re usually walking thousands of extra steps, climbing stairs, and moving throughout the day instead of driving everywhere. That extra activity adds up and supports digestion and energy balance.

6. Less stress and more relaxation. Vacations often mean lower stress, better sleep, and more time to enjoy meals, all of which can influence digestion.

The takeaway: You don’t have to move to Italy. You can recreate many of these habits at home—choose 100% durum wheat semolina pasta, cook it al dente, make simple sauces, eat reasonable portions, slow down during meals, and build more walking into your day.

Lead in lunchables? Let’s put this risk into perspective.

Lead may be present in food from the environment where foods are grown, raised, or processed. Levels of lead in the environment can vary depending on natural geographical makeup and proximity to current or past use or manufacturing of products made with lead. For example, lead has entered the environment from the past widespread use of lead in paint, gasoline, and plumbing materials, as well as many other products. While many commercial and industrial uses of lead have been phased out, there are still some products used or made in the U.S. that contain lead, and it is still used in products made in other countries.

Because there is no known safe level of exposure to lead, the FDA monitors and regulates levels of lead in foods. While it is not possible to completely prevent lead from entering the food supply, for foods that contain lead, it may be possible to reduce the levels through changes to agricultural or manufacturing practices. By law, food manufacturers have a responsibility to significantly minimize or prevent chemical hazards when needed. 

An interim reference level (IRL) is a benchmark the FDA may use to determine if the amount of exposure to the contaminant in food is a potential health concern. IRLs also may be used to inform action levels, which are the level of contaminant in a food above which the FDA may consider a food harmful to health and in violation of the FDA’s safety laws.

Why does your menstrual cycle make you poop more? 

If your bowel habits completely change around your menstrual cycle, there’s actually a reason for it.

During menstruation, your body produces higher levels of prostaglandins. These chemicals help your uterus contract, but they don’t only affect the uterus—they can also stimulate your intestines.

When your colon contracts more, stool moves through your digestive tract faster. That means less water is absorbed, which can lead to loose stools, diarrhea, urgency, or going to the bathroom more often.

A few things that may help:

• Sip peppermint tea to help relax the muscles of the digestive tract.

• Fennel tea may help with menstrual discomfort and cramping.

• Ginger tea has been shown in studies to reduce menstrual cramps and may also help settle your stomach.

• Eat more soluble fiber, including oats, psyllium husk, and chia seeds. Soluble fiber absorbs water and can help improve stool consistency.

• Consider cutting back on caffeine if it tends to make your symptoms worse.

• Make sure you’re getting enough calcium-rich foods, including dairy or fortified non-dairy alternatives. Adequate calcium intake has been linked to fewer menstrual symptoms.

• Diets that are lower in fat and higher in vegetarian or plant-based foods have also been associated with less painful periods in some studies.

Period poops are incredibly common, and for most people they’re simply a normal response to hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle.

More info on human health risk assessments: Test durations are acute, subchronic, and chronic. Acute toxicity testing involves short-term tests with a single exposure. Subchronic testing involves intermediate-length exposures to multiple doses for periods ranging from 30 to 90 days. Chronic testing considers long-term exposures to consecutive, repeated doses over most of the test animal’s life span. Chronic testing evaluates the potential to cause damage to organs and organ systems and the potential to cause cancer in addition to a set of tests to assess the potential for a pesticide to damage DNA that also informs assessments of potential carcinogenicity.

Studies to define how a pesticide is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted by mammals are also required. These tests provide an understanding of whether the pesticide will accumulate in the body, be present in milk, or be metabolized into a form that presents unique safety concerns. Testing also considers developmental and reproductive toxicity to evaluate the potential to cause fetal toxicity and birth defects as well as their ability to mimic hormones or otherwise disrupt hormonal signaling.

RfD or ADI values, which are reported in units of milligrams of pesticide per kilogram of body weight per day (mg/kg/day), can be interpreted as the amount of a particular compound a person may consume every day without raising concerns for adverse effects. The sum of all exposures to a pesticide or class of pesticides across all approved uses cannot exceed the RfD.

It’s okay to add a banana to your blueberry smoothie. Bananas are nutritious, I eat them, and this is not a reason to stop. But if your goal is to preserve as many of the berry polyphenols as possible, the chemistry matters. 
 
A small, acute study in eight healthy men compared standardized cocoa flavan-3-ols consumed alone, in a banana smoothie, or in a mixed-berry smoothie. The banana smoothie reduced circulating epicatechin metabolites by approximately 80%, whereas the berry smoothie produced levels similar to the flavan-3-ols consumed alone. 

The culprit was polyphenol oxidase, or PPO, an enzyme that oxidizes certain polyphenols when plant tissue is blended. 

- Banana: approximately 3,258 units of PPO activity per 100 grams
- Avocado: approximately 24 units per 100 grams
- Blueberry: approximately 12 units per 100 grams

This does not mean a banana eliminates every beneficial compound in blueberries. Blueberries contain many other polyphenols, including anthocyanins, and this was a small study that should be replicated. But the magnitude of the effect was meaningful enough for me to consider when optimizing my smoothie. 

My solution is simple: I replace the banana with avocado. 
 
Per 100 grams, avocado contains approximately 95% less sugar, more than twice the fiber, about 36% more potassium, and more folate, vitamin K, and niacin than banana. It also contains substantially more monounsaturated fat (and therefore more calories) which may not align with everyone’s goals. 
 
For me, that fat is another advantage. I add kale to my smoothie, which is rich in lutein. Lutein accumulates in the retina and the brain, where it contributes to visual and cognitive function. Human studies have found that adding avocado to a carotenoid-rich meal can substantially increase lutein (more than 5-fold) and beta-carotene absorption. 

So this is not about labeling bananas as “bad.” It is about matching the ingredient to the objective, which is polyphenol optimization (for me).

One of the things I think about more as I get older is physical reserve.

I want to preserve the muscle and cardiorespiratory fitness that let me keep doing the things I enjoy. And the reality is that these capacities are often easier to maintain than they are to rebuild after they have been lost.

That is part of why I train with so much variety!

This home-gym circuit mixed loaded squats and lunges, carries, burpees, core and single-leg work, rowing, shuttle runs, the Echo bike, and cable work. It might look like a random assortment of exercises, but the variety is intentional. Different movements challenge different qualities—strength, power, balance, coordination, endurance, and the ability to produce and absorb force.

Loaded exercises create mechanical tension, one of the primary signals for muscle growth and remodeling. Resistance and impact also place strain on the skeleton, which helps stimulate the ongoing process of bone remodeling. Single-leg and lateral movements challenge stability, coordination, and movement.

The vigorous intervals provide a different stimulus. The rapid increase in energy demand activates pathways involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, and over time, these adaptations can improve the muscle’s capacity to produce energy and sustain demanding work.

Lactate rises too, and it can be used as a fuel and also acts as a signaling molecule. Exercise-induced lactate production has been linked with the acute rise in BDNF, a protein involved in brain plasticity.

Of course, one workout does not suddenly create new muscle, stronger bones, more mitochondria, and a more resilient brain. Those adaptations require a repeated dose, enough intensity and progression over time, followed by enough protein, sleep, and recovery (where the rebuilding actually happens).

When you train this way, the body receives a recurring message to preserve muscle, bone, power, aerobic capacity, balance, and many of the other functional qualities that become increasingly important with age.

I think of it as biological insurance for keeping the capacities that make a longer life more functional and more enjoyable!

High fructose corn syrup doesn’t have to be labeled as high fructose corn syrup anymore!?

The issue is not the more accurate labeling of “fructose,” but the many misconceptions regarding high fructose corn syrup that allow “no high fructose corn syrup” to be an effective marketing label. 

A common misconception is that HFCS is “high” in fructose compared to most sweeteners, but the truth is that it’s only “high” in fructose compared to the corn syrup it was derived from, which is purely glucose. HFCS-55 contains a similar ratio of fructose to glucose as both sugar (sucrose) and honey, and HFCS-42 is even lower in fructose than all of the other options. Pure sucrose is 50 percent fructose and 50 percent glucose, which is chemically bound. This chemical bond is rapidly broken down by the sucrase enzyme in the intestine, which releases fructose and glucose for absorption. HFCS often gets confused with pure fructose, which it is not.

Studies comparing intake of sucrose, HFCS, and other similar sweeteners such as honey have found they exert similar metabolic effects.

There is NO ‘best’ rep range for building muscle

The idea that you must do 8-12 reps for muscle growth because that is the ‘hypertrophy rep range’ is NOT supported by research data

Current research consistently shows that muscle growth is similar across a very wide range of rep ranges (roughly 3-30 reps), provided that:
 ✅ Sets are taken sufficiently close to failure
 ✅ Training volume is similar
 ✅ Technique is solid

That doesn’t mean all rep ranges are interchangeable.

Heavy, lower-rep training is generally more time-efficient and better for building maximal strength, but it places higher mechanical loads on joints and connective tissue (PMIDs: 33312275 & 28834797).

Higher-rep training reduces the load you have to lift, but it often creates more local fatigue and discomfort before the target muscle is fully challenged (PMID; 32401690).

The “best” rep range isn’t a magic number, it’s the one that lets you train hard, recover well, stay consistent, and progressively overload over months and years. It’s also a rep range that you enjoy doing and will be consistent with

Stop chasing the perfect rep range. Start chasing progressive overload and consistency.

The best sleep strategy for athletic performance is not a complicated “hack.” In fact, the top tips are surprisingly simple.

Here are the top recommendations from my conversation with sleep expert Dr. Michael Grandner:

1. Experiment with getting slightly more sleep.

Sleep-extension studies in young athletes consistently show improvements in performance. But rather than suddenly spending an extra hour in bed, move bedtime earlier by about 15 minutes at a time and see whether you can actually sleep during that window.

2. Bank sleep before competition.

Prioritize sleep during the week or two leading into an important event. Many athletes sleep poorly the night before a race or competition. That is much less concerning when you arrive well-rested rather than already carrying accumulated sleep loss.

3. Do not panic over one bad night.

One or two short nights generally will not destroy performance when you are coming from a strong baseline. The stress and anxiety about not sleeping may sometimes be more disruptive than the lost sleep itself.

4. Think in patterns, not isolated nights.

Sleep is a lot like nutrition. One excellent night cannot completely undo a chronically poor routine, and one bad night does not erase weeks of consistency.

The night before matters much less than most athletes think. The sleep you consistently accumulate beforehand is what creates resilience when race- or competition-day nerves inevitably show up.

Let’s talk about booster shots, and why not every vaccine needs another dose.

Some vaccines provide protection that fades over time and require additional doses to maintain that protection. For example, tetanus and diphtheria protection declines over time, so adults need a Td or Tdap booster dose about every 10 years. Tdap is also recommended in every pregnancy so your baby has some protection against pertussis before they’re born. Measles is a different story. Once you’ve had the recommended doses, you’re covered for life. Flu and COVID vaccines aren’t exactly booster shots. They get updated each season to match what’s circulating, which is why they come around every year.
